en: Homage be to Manu, Vācaspati, Śukra, Parāśara with his son, and to the learned Cāṇakya— to all the authors of treatises on statecraft for kings.
(As it is heard: There is, in the southern region, a city named Mahilāropya.

Therein lived a king named Amaraśakti, who was like a wish-granting tree for the desires of all supplicants; whose pair of feet was colored by the mass of rays from the jewels in the crowns of the most eminent kings; who had reached the further shore of all arts (*kalā*) [and was learned in all treatises on worldly affairs];
and who possessed three sons—Vasuśakti, Ugraśakti, and Anekaśakti—who were of exceedingly dull intellect.

Then, observing that they were dull-witted regarding the science of polity (*arthaśāstra*), the king summoned his ministers and deliberated: "It is already known to you how these sons of mine are exceedingly dull-witted. What is the purpose of a son being born who is neither learned nor righteous?"
What is done with that cow which neither yields milk nor bears calves?
Better is a miscarriage; better is not approaching one's wife during her fertile seasons;
better is a stillborn child; and better even is it to give birth to a daughter alone.
Better is a barren wife, better is dwelling without a home, than a son who lacks wisdom, even if he is endowed with beauty, wealth, and strength.
(4) (5) "Therefore, by what means can the awakening of their intellect be accomplished? (Thus [he thought].)

(6) Regarding this, some said: "Your Majesty, it is said that grammar (*vyākaraṇa*) is mastered in twelve years. If that can somehow be understood, then the treatises on Dharma, Artha, and Kāma should be studied. But this is exceedingly profound even for the wise, let alone for those of dull intellect. (7) "In this matter, there is a Brahmin named Viṣṇuśarman who knows the essence of all the treatises on political ethics (*nītiśāstra*) and whose fame is celebrated among many disciples.
Summon him and entrust the princes to him."
When this had been done, the king summoned by his ministers greeted him with a blessing appropriate for a twice-born man and he sat down. Once he was seated comfortably, the king said to him:

"O Brahmin, for the sake of favoring me, you ought to make these princes—who are dull-witted—unrivaled in the science of polity (*arthaśāstra*). And I shall honor you with a suitable measure of wealth.
When the monarch had spoken thus, Viṣṇuśarman also rose and addressed the king:

"Your Majesty, please hear this proclamation of my words: I do not speak thus out of a desire for wealth, nor is there any time for me—being eighty years old and with all my senses declined—to enjoy any worldly objects. Rather, this undertaking is intentional, for your sake. Therefore, let this day be recorded.
If, within six months, I do not make your sons masters of the science of polity (*nītiśāstra*), then you ought to have me dragged a hundred paces away by the hand as a lesson in the path."

Having heard this seemingly impossible promise of the Brahmin, the king, together with his ministers, was filled with joy and wonder; and out of great respect, he entrusted the princes to Viṣṇuśarman.

He, in turn, having devised five treatises (*tantra*) by means of stories—namely, *The Separation of Friends*, *The Acquisition of Friends*, *The Crows and the Owls*, *Loss of Gains*, and *Hasty Action Without Examination*—began to instruct the princes in the science of polity (*nītiśāstra*).
[This concludes the "Introduction to the Stories."]
Now begins the first tantra, titled "The Breach of Friendship.
Its opening verse is as follows:
"A great friendship between a lion and a bull grew ever stronger in the forest."
"He was destroyed by a jackal who was both treacherous and excessively greedy.
The princes asked, "How was that? Viṣṇuśarman related:
"In the southern region, there is a city named Mahilāropya."
There lived a caravan leader named Vardhamānaka, who earned his livelihood through righteous means.
Once, a thought arose in him: "Even though my wealth is abundant, I must still increase my fortune. And it is said:

One should seek wealth not yet obtained, protect what has been obtained with vigilance, increase what has been protected constantly, and bestow what has been increased upon worthy recipients. (This is the worldly course: "The acquisition of what is not yet obtained, the protection of what has been obtained, the increase of what has been protected, and the dedication of what has been increased to the proper field. In this regard: for one who does not obtain anything, there is nothing at all; even wealth that has been obtained perishes immediately if it is not protected due to many calamities; and wealth that is not increased, even if used sparingly, is exhausted like collyrium; [if it is not used at all... [9]
"In the production of wealth, it is equal to not having acquired it at all. (8) Therefore, one should apply oneself to the protection and increase of what has been acquired. And it is said:
"Indeed, for wealth that has been acquired, renunciation is its true preservation."
Like an outflow for waters situated within a tank or a cavern;

(9) having thus reflected, and having gathered the merchandise destined for Mathurā, he departed from that city for the sake of trade on an auspicious lunar day, with the permission of his elders. [10]
He departed.
He had two bulls for his draft animals, named Vohāra, Ara, Nandaka, and Sañjīvaka.

Now, as he was traveling through a great forest, the ground became muddy with water that had been obstructed by the impact of mountains and difficult trees; moreover, the cart suffered from the exhaustion of its single axle and the excessive weight of its heavy load. Then, at a certain spot, by the power of fate, Sañjīvaka broke the yoke and sat down.
Seeing him, the caravan leader Vardhamānaka fell into great despair.
When he had fasted for three days and still did not regain his health,
he then appointed guards over him [to protect the rest of the caravan].
Thinking, "The forest is a place of danger," he departed for another region as he desired.
On another day, out of fear of him, the guards approached and told him a lie: "Master, that Saṃjīvaka is dead, and we have honored him with fire and other rites.
Having heard this, the caravan leader, out of gratitude, performed the funeral rites for him and departed.
Saṃjīvaka, too, because some life remained within him, had his body restored by the extremely cooling waters mixed with moisture; having somehow risen, he gradually approached the bank of the Yamunā.

There, grazing on the tips of young grass that resembled emeralds and wandering at will, after a few days he became strong, with a thick hump like that of Śiva’s bull, his limbs robust and flourishing, and he remained there daily bellowing as he scraped the mounds of anthills with the tips of his horns.

Now, in that forest, not far away, a lion named Piṅgalaka dwelt in the heart of the woods, surrounded by all kinds of wild animals. Carrying his head high without fear, he enjoyed the pleasures of a kingdom acquired through his own prowess. And so it is said: [13] "To one who dwells alone in the forest, devoid of royal insignia, yet knowing the scriptures..."
When a king is exalted by his majesty, words take on their true meaning. No consecration and no ritual refinement is performed for the lion by the beasts;
his sovereignty over the kings of beasts is won of its own accord through his valor.
Once, overcome by thirst and seeking water, he descended to the bank of the Yamunā.
From afar, he heard the roar of Sañjīvaka— which had never been heard before— resembling the deep thundering of a cloud at the time of the dissolution of the world.

Having heard that, with an unagitated heart, he did not drink the water; concealing his intention, he remained silent in the area of the maṇḍala-vrata, standing in the arrangement of the four maṇḍalas.

(22) This is the arrangement of the four circles (*maṇḍala*): namely, the Lion, the Lion’s Followers, the Crows, and the "How-Dare-They" (*kiṃvṛtta*). Among all these—whether in villages, cities, towns, capitals, market towns, hamlets, parks, monasteries, forests, groves, or forest clearings—the Lion alone is the resident lord. A few followers of the Lion are the *tantrādhara*s. The groups of crows are the middle-ranking group. Those who dwell in other locations are the "How-Dare-They. (23) He had two sons of ministers named Karaṭaka and Damanaka, who were jackals.

(24) (The two of them consulted with one another. Thereupon Damanaka said to Karaṭaka: "My good Karaṭaka, for what reason has our master Piṅgalaka, who has set out to fetch water, stopped here? (25) Karaṭaka replied: "What business of ours is this? And it is said:
'He who desires to involve himself in matters that are not his own business lies dead, like the monkey who pulled out the wedge. 6.
(26) Damanaka said: "How was that? He replied:
[16] "In a certain region, near a city, a merchant had begun to construct a temple.
There, the laborers—the architects and others—would enter the middle of the city at midday for the sake of food."

Now, there was a half-split wooden pillar made of *arjuna* wood belonging to a certain craftsman, which remained standing, held in place by a *khadira* wood peg driven through its center as a mechanical support.
Once, a large troop of forest-dwelling monkeys arrived, playing at will here and there among the tree-tops, palace roofs, and piles of timber.

In that situation, one monkey (who was on the verge of destruction), out of innate restlessness, sat upon a pillar and hung his testicles into its hole. Thinking, "Who has driven this peg into such an improper place?", he seized it with both hands and endeavored to pull it out.
What happened when the peg moved from its place is already known to you, even though it was not told by me.
Therefore I say: "One should avoid involvement in the affairs of others. Thus it is said.
"For our part, we have already consumed all our food.
Damanaka said: "How is it that you seek only food? Everyone strives to serve a superior for the sake of some special gain. And this is well said: 'For the sake of benefiting friends...'"
Even for those who are enemies, seeking the patronage of a king is desired by the wise for the sake of warding off harm;
for who does not merely sustain their belly? 7.[19]
He in whose living many live, he indeed truly lives;
even a crane fills its own belly with its beak—what does it not do? Furthermore:
even a cow's bone, though devoid of flesh and filthy, being left with only a small amount of sinew and fat...
A dog attains satisfaction upon finding [something], yet that does not appease its hunger;
a lion kills a leopard even while abandoning a jackal that has come into its very lap.
Indeed, every person, even when fallen into distress, desires that which is appropriate to their own nature.
The fruit:
wagging the tail, stamping the feet on the ground, falling prostrate, and showing the face and belly.

A dog eats the morsel of one who gives it; an elephant, however, looks about with steady composure and eats with its four tusks. But that man here who eats what is produced by learning and valor—he truly eats well.
Even a dog, it is said, receives an offering by merely wagging its own tail.
But that life which is lived even for a moment by men renowned for wisdom, valor, and fame, and whose pride remains unbroken— that alone is truly lived.
Those who know the truth declare that such a life here is not true living;
even a crow lives for a long time and eats the offerings of Bali. A small stream is easily filled, and the paws of a mouse are easily filled. 12.20 [20]
A base person is easily satisfied even with very little;
his intellect is devoid of discernment between the harmful and the beneficial,
and he is excluded from the many traditions of sacred learning.
What difference is there between a beast and a human-beast who is solely intent on filling his belly? (14) [The former is one who eats grass and bears the heavy yoke of the master’s cart.]
And that lord of bulls, who plows through both even and uneven ground, purifying the world’s implements, is distinguished above the human beast. (15)

(36) Karaṭaka said: "We two are, after all, not the primary ones; therefore, what is the use of this task for us? (37) He replied: "My good friend, in how much time does even one who is not primary become primary? And it is said: [21]
In this world, no one becomes eminent, esteemed, or wicked by virtue of their own power; rather, it is through the influence of others that one attains either the status of a teacher or the opposite.
It is one's own actions alone that lead men [to their fate]. 16.
Just as a stone is raised to the mountain peak with great effort, yet falls down easily, so too is the self [elevated or cast down] by virtue and vice. 17.
"Therefore, my good friend, the self of everyone is indeed dependent upon oneself.
Karataka said: "Then what do you intend to do here?
He replied: "This master Piṅgalaka is first of all timid, his retinue is likewise timid, and he is of dull intellect."
He said: "How do you know this?
Damanaka replied: "What is there to be known here?
And it has been said: [22]
An expressed meaning is understood even by a beast;
horses and elephants carry when urged;
and a wise person infers even that which is unspoken.
For the intellects of others bear fruit through the knowledge of their gestures.
Therefore, this very day I shall make him my own by means of the power of wisdom.
Karaṭaka said: "My good sir, you are ignorant of the principles of service."
Damanaka said: "My good sir, how could I be unacquainted with service? Indeed, I have mastered the entire duty of a subordinate. And it is said:
What is too heavy for the capable? What is too far for the persevering?
What is a foreign land for the well-educated? Who is a stranger to those who speak kindly? [23]
Karataka said: "Perhaps the master will despise you for entering at an inappropriate time.
He replied: "That is indeed true; nevertheless, one must certainly remain in the presence of a servant. And it has been said:

The king usually favors a person who is close at hand, even if they lack learning, lack noble birth, or have no reputation. Kings and the creepers of negligence alike embrace whoever dwells by their side. (20)
"Servants who investigate the treasures of anger and favor gradually ascend even to a king who is shaking them off.
Karataka said: "Then, having gone there, what will your honor say?
Damanaka replied:
Each subsequent statement arises from the preceding one, just as a further seed is produced from a seed endowed with the quality of a good rain. (Moreover:
[It wards off] the calamity born from the sight of misfortune.
And the wise, employing the methods of policy, display success born from the perception of means as if it were shimmering before them. 23.
And I shall not speak at an improper time. For one who speaks at an improper time, even if he were Bṛhaspati himself, gains only the contempt of others and sheer disdain for his intelligence. 24.
He does not speak at an improper place, at an improper time, to one whose faculties are unripe, or to one devoid of virtue; for how could his well-spoken discourse ever be fruitless? 25.
Moreover:
[25] That by which one maintains one's livelihood and for which one is praised by the virtuous in an assembly—that quality should be increased and protected by the possessor of that quality.
Karaṭaka said: "Indeed, kings are difficult to propitiate; like mountains, they are perpetually rugged by nature, full of pitfalls, seekers of vulnerabilities, and graspers of deceit."
"Kings are like serpents: they possess wealth, they are clad in armor, they are cruel, they move in crooked ways, and they are to be subdued by spells.
He replied: "It is even so.
Nevertheless, those men who are truly skilled serve even a king, consume even poison, and take pleasure with women."
"For whatever disposition a man possesses, by entering into him through that very disposition, a wise person may quickly bring him under their own control.
Karaṭaka said: "May your paths be auspicious; proceed as you intend.
Then Damanaka, having taken leave of him, went slowly toward Piṅgalaka.

There, seeing Damanaka approaching even from afar, Piṅgalaka said to the doorkeeper: "Let there be no hesitation; let the cane-staff be removed. Here is our long-standing minister’s son, Damanaka, who has arrived. For he is one whose entry is unimpeded, as he belongs to the second circle.
Then Damanaka approached, bowed, and sat down.
And he, preceded by pride, said:
"It has been a long time since we last saw you.
Damanaka replied: "Your Majesty has no need for me whatsoever."
Nevertheless, that which is appropriate for the occasion must certainly be spoken, because there is no purpose for kings that is not served by some [advice].
And it has been said: [28]
O King,
for horses, there is need for a toothpick or even a blade of grass to scratch their ears.
How much less, then, could a man with merely his voice and hands [accomplish it]?
Moreover:
for even when one whose conduct is steadfast is treated with contempt...
The quality of fortitude cannot be wiped away,
for even when turned downward, the flames of fire never go below. 31.
Should he not be dealt with once his poison has been neutralized? 32.
Always be a connoisseur of the distinctions between the kingdom and its people; for prosperity is indeed dependent solely upon knowledge of those internal matters. 33. [29]

A farmer, having thoroughly mixed all the seeds, should sow them; he should discern the true nature of the seed that has been produced by means of the sprout. Therefore, a master must always be one who possesses specialized knowledge. And so it is said:
Servants and provisions should be assigned only to their proper places; for a crest-jewel is not bound upon the foot on the grounds of its power. It is fit for the wearing of golden ornaments.
If a gem is set in tin, it neither shines nor is it unattractive; rather, the blame falls upon the one who made the setting. [30]

A king who understands how to distinguish between his servants—knowing, "This one is intelligent and devoted; this one is fearless; this one is dull-witted"—is surrounded by servants. Yet, when he is treated as an equal by those who are not his equals, and when his honors are diminished by those who are his equals, [he falls into ruin]. 37.

A servant who is deprived of his duties abandons his master for three reasons. (38) Where there is no distinction between the left and right hands, what noble person would dwell there even for a moment, when a way out exists? (39) [31]
There is a vast difference between horses, elephants, and iron; between wood, stone, and cloth; and between women and men.
Indeed, he who desires to carry a thousand loads of stone upon his shoulders [is like one who attempts the impossible].
Exertion leads either to destruction or to that which is devoid of wisdom; it carries one away from the goal. 42.
Having obtained a ruby the size of a thumb’s joint—a gem distinguished by its excellence, easy to carry, and of supreme value—does one not thereby attain his purpose? 43.
A horse, a weapon, a scripture, a lute, speech, a man, and a woman—
these become either unworthy or worthy depending on the particular individual who possesses them.
(44) And as for this contemptuous disregard shown toward me, thinking, "This is a jackal," [it is misplaced].
That too is incorrect, because: Why is Viṣṇu in the form of a boar, the Great Seer in the form of a deer, and the Six-faced One in the form of a goat not worshipped by the virtuous? (45.32)
It is not established as an absolute rule that a long-standing servant born in the house is always beneficial, while a minister who is discreet is so;
for even a mouse, though born in the house, must be killed if it is harmful.
A cat, though beneficial, is sought out by others only through the offering of bribes.
Just as there is no use for wood in the work of a carpenter even when eranda, bhiṇḍa, arka, and nala plants are gathered in great abundance, so too there is no purpose served by the ignorant.
"What is the use of one who is devoted but incapable, or one who is capable but harmful?
O King, you ought to know me as I truly am—both devoted and capable.
Because of a king's lack of discernment, his retinue becomes devoid of intelligence."
Consequently, because of their predominance, wise men do not remain nearby;
when the kingdom is abandoned by the wise, political policy does not become virtuous;
and when policy has perished, the entire family, being powerless, comes to ruin.
Piṅgalaka said: "My good friend (Damanaka), do not speak thus. You are our minister’s son from long ago.
Damanaka said: "Your Majesty, there is something that must be said.
He replied: "Speak what you wish to say."
Damanaka said: "The master has set out for the purpose of fetching water; why then has he returned here and remained as if astonished, without even drinking any water?
Piṅgalaka, in order to conceal his true state, said: "Dama—" [34]

[He said: "No, there is no reason at all. (68) He replied: "My Lord, if it is truly not to be told, then let it be. (69) Nevertheless, Piṅgalaka, having heard this, reflected: '(I have been noticed by him; he appears to be capable. Why then should I hide anything from this devoted one? I shall tell him my intention first. And he said: (70) 'O Damanaka, listen to this great sound from afar. He [Damanaka] said: 'Master, the sound has clearly been heard. What of it? Piṅgalaka said: (71) 'Good sir, I wish to depart from this forest. For this reason: some unprecedented creature has entered here, of whom this great and unprecedented sound is heard. The creature must correspond to the sound, and the prowess must correspond to the creature. Therefore, [all—]"
"How then should we remain here? (72) Damanaka said: "Why has fear come upon you, Master, from a mere sound? That too is improper. Moreover:

A dam is breached by water; likewise, a secret counsel is ruined when unprotected. Affection is broken by slander; a coward is undone by words. (51) (73) Therefore, it is not fitting for my Master to [lose] what was previously acquired based on a mere sound."

This forest is to be abandoned. For here, indeed, various kinds of sounds are heard; yet these are merely sounds, not causes for fear. For example: (the sounds of thundering clouds, flutes, lutes, cymbals, drums, conchs, bells, carts, doors, machines, and so forth are heard), and one should not be afraid of them. And it has been said: "I already knew this before; indeed, this place is full of fat. Having entered within, I have realized that it is nothing but skin and wood. (52)
Piṅgalaka said: "How was that? Damanaka replied:
"There was a certain jackal, his throat parched with hunger, who, while wandering here and there in search of food, saw the battlefield of two armies in the forest. And there he heard a great noise.
His heart agitated by fear, he thought: 'What is this? I am lost! Whose is this sound, where does it come from, and what kind of creature is it?'"
Then, as he was searching, he saw a drum shaped like a mountain peak.
Upon seeing it, he thought: "Is this sound inherent to it, or is it produced by something else?
Then, when it was struck by the tips of tree branches driven by the wind, it made a sound; otherwise, it remained silent.
Desiring to know all of her secrets, he went near her;

out of curiosity, he himself struck both their faces [with his hand], and thought: "Aha! After a long time, this great feast has arrived for me. It must surely be filled with abundant flesh, fat, and blood."
Then, having torn open the mouth of a drum, he entered within;
yet, because the hide was so tough, he somehow failed to break his fangs.
Even there, he found nothing at all.
Turning back (while inwardly laughing), he said: "I already knew this.
Therefore, I say: one should not fear merely because of a sound.
(89) However, if you think, "I shall go to where this sound is in order to understand its true nature," [then do so].
(90) Piṅgalaka said: "Are you able to go into his presence?
He replied, "Certainly.
Piṅgalaka said: "My good friend, if that is so, then go; may your paths be auspicious."
(91) Damanaka also, having bowed to him, set out in pursuit of the sound of Sañjīvaka.
(92) Then, after Damanaka had departed, Piṅgalaka, his mind agitated by fear, reflected: "Alas, I have not done well, in that I placed my trust in him and revealed my own intention."

He was informed: (93) "Perhaps this Damanaka, having become a double-agent, might harbor evil intentions toward me. (94) And it is said: One who has been honored and then insulted, one who has been rejected, one who is angry, one who is greedy, one who is impoverished, or one who has come of his own accord—such a person can be won over by means of a stratagem.

One who is excessively attached to his own status, one defeated after being summoned, one insulted by those of equal skill in their craft, one tormented by exile, one eclipsed by equals, one whose honor has been snatched away, and likewise one whose legal affairs have been subverted; those who desire the destruction of their kin and do not waver from their own duties even in an assembly, and who act with deceit on all sides—thinking "I am such a one whose honor has been snatched away," he might perhaps undergo a transformation toward me.

He might submit, or else, being pursued by a stronger force due to his own lack of capability, he might pass through my very midst. (Even so, I would be ruined. (95) Therefore, I shall resort to another place from this spot until I have ascertained what he intends to do; having thus resolved, he went to another location and stood there alone, watching Damanaka’s path. (96) Damanaka, too, having gone to Sañjīvaka’s side and recognized him as "this bull," set out toward Piṅgalaka with a joyful heart. (97) Piṅgalaka had returned to his former position in order to conceal his true state of mind; otherwise, Damanaka would think, "This king is a coward, and his retinue is likewise cowardly. (98) Damanaka, having approached Piṅgalaka, bowed and sat down. [42]
Piṅgalaka said: "Was that creature seen by you?
Damanaka replied: "It was seen, [by the grace of my lord].
Piṅgalaka said: "Was it seen exactly as it is?"
Damanaka said, "It was seen exactly as it is.
He replied, "It was not seen exactly as it is. For this reason: you are not the primary cause, and because you lack power, there is no one above you who can obstruct him.

As it is said: 'The wind does not uproot the tender grasses that are lowly and bowed down on all sides; rather, it strikes down only the trees that stand tall. The great exercise their prowess only against those who are great. "

"Moreover: Even though struck by the soles of the feet of a swarming bee intoxicated by the increase of rut-fluid on his temples, an elephant—though possessed of extreme strength—does not give way to anger; yet those who are equal in strength provoke the anger of one who is stronger. (102) Damanaka said: "I already knew beforehand what my lord would say. So, what is the use of much talk? I shall bring him here into your presence. (103) Hearing this, Piṅgalaka said joyfully: "Let it be done immediately!"
(104) Damanaka went back again and spoke to Saṃjīvaka reproachfully:
(105) "Come, come, you wicked bull! Your master Piṅgalaka calls for you, saying: 'Why do you bellow so uselessly again and again as if you were fearless?
(106) Having heard that, Saṃjīvaka said: "My good friend, who is this Piṅgalaka by name who speaks to me?"
(Then, laughing with astonishment) Damanaka said to him: "How is it that you do not even know your master Piṅgalaka?
(He replied indignantly: "You shall know by the fruit.")
"Indeed, here stands Piṅgalaka, the king of beasts, the lord of all animals, surrounded by his retinue and seated in a majestic array; he is haughty in mind, a master, a great lion.
Upon hearing this, Saṃjīvaka, considering himself as good as dead, fell into extreme despondency and said:
"If I must certainly come, then please grant me the gift of safety."

[111] Having agreed, saying, "So be it," Damanaka went to Siṃha, informed him of the matter, and having received his permission, he led Saṃjīvaka, who had acted as instructed, into the presence of Piṅgalaka.
[113] Placing his right paw—thick, rounded, long, and adorned with claws like diamond ornaments—upon him, he spoke with great courtesy:
[114] "Is it well with you? From where have you come to this desolate forest?"
[115] Thus questioned, Saṃjīvaka related his previous history, beginning from his birth in the lineage of caravan leaders down to his separation [from them].

[116] Having heard this, Piṅgalaka said to him: "Friend, you must not fear; dwell here in this forest, which is protected by my own arms, according to your custom. Furthermore, you must remain constantly by my side. For what reason? This forest is full of many dangers due to its teeming with numerous fierce creatures. Saṃjīvaka replied: "As Your Majesty commands."
[117] Having spoken thus, Piṅgalaka, surrounded by all his deer, [118] thereafter spent his time with Piṅgalaka and Sañjīvaka in mutual affection every day.
[119] Because Sañjīvaka’s intellect was refined by the meaning of many treatises, Piṅgalaka—though previously ignorant due to his wild nature—was made wise in a very short time.
[120] To say more, Piṅgalaka and Sañjīvaka alone would deliberate on secret matters every day; all the rest of the deer population remained at a distance.
[121] And because they were deprived of food by the lion’s display of prowess, Karaṭaka and Damanaka, being tormented by hunger, reflected upon one another.
(122) Thereupon Damanaka said: "My dear Karataka, we are both ruined. What, then, should be done here? [He spoke thus] by himself.
This fault was committed by you who brought Saṃjīvaka into the presence of Piṅgalaka. And it has been said:
"The jackal through the fight of rams, we through Ṣāḍhabhūti, and the messenger through the intrigue—these three misfortunes were brought about by ourselves. [48]
Karaṭaka said, "How was that? He replied:
"In a certain region there lived a wandering mendicant named Devaśarman.
Through the accumulation over time of many fine garments obtained from various virtuous people, he came to possess a great quantity of wealth."

(And he did not place his trust in anyone. Then, once upon a time, a thief of others' wealth named Āṣāḍhabhūti, having noticed that amount of wealth situated within his [the king's] armpit, reflected: "How can this amount of wealth belonging to him be taken away by me? Having thus deliberated, he began to attend upon him and, in the course of time, gained his confidence.
Then, on one occasion, while that wandering mendicant was engaged in a pilgrimage, he [was accompanied] by that Āṣāḍhabhūti.
He began to travel together with them.

(Fie, you fool! By your excessive wisdom, you have consumed your own lineage. And well said is this:

The face of a wicked man, like that of a serpent—twisted-tongued, causing agitation, cruel, and utterly ruthless—is intended solely for doing harm.

Therefore, since you bring your own master to such a state, to him you are as insignificant as a blade of grass.

In a certain locality, there was a merchant’s son whose wealth had been exhausted.

Not far from there was a river; as he prepared to bathe there, he sent his own son after him, equipped with an *āmalaka* fruit and a bathing cloth. Having bathed, that man returned and [found] the boy at the house of another friend.

Thus questioned by the officials of justice,

Wisdom in one who has heard much is like oil upon water; poison [is contained] within blood; intimacy with the virtuous [is found] among those who love their kin; secrets are betrayed among the undisciplined; and in this world, the reputation of the famous rests upon virtuous people.
Goodness is not the inherent nature of a man;
for embodied beings, fame is rooted in conduct.

And as for the fact that you are constantly devoted to the highest virtues—even that very nature pulls you back. How so?

Where there is evidence that you are not present, that action would not be auspicious.

that which is improper is simply improper;

One who commits violence against living beings should be executed by a king desiring prosperity.
A compassionate king, a Brahmin who eats all things, a woman who is not self-controlled, and a companion of evil character—[these are to be avoided]. 173.
A servant who is rebellious, an official who is negligent,
and one who does not acknowledge what has been done for him— these should be abandoned.
A kingdom cannot be governed by one who possesses the nature of an ordinary man.

For those very faults that belong to ordinary men are the virtues of a king. (176) [180] He may speak truth or falsehood, be harsh or pleasant in speech, cruel or compassionate, intent on wealth or generous.
"Constantly expending wealth yet receiving abundant and diverse inflows of riches,
the king is like a courtesan, assuming many forms.

Thus ends the first chapter, titled "The Separation of Friends.
Now begins the second chapter, titled "The Acquisition of Friends," of which this is the first verse:
Those who lack resources and are destitute of wealth, yet possess intelligence and the counsel of friends, quickly accomplish their tasks—just like the crow, the tortoise, the deer, and the mouse.
The princes asked, "How was that? Viṣṇuśarman related:
In the southern country there is a city named Mahilāropya.
Not far from it stood a great silk-cotton tree (*śālmalī*), thick with trunks and branches. Therein lived a bird named Laghupatanaka.
Once, having set out for food at the time of dawn, he saw a creature of fierce form, with water in its trunk, like a second Kāla armed with a staff of wood, striking at birds to bind them.
Seeing him, he became apprehensive and thought:
"What will this one do to us?"
Thus he remained, filled with curiosity:
"What does this evil-minded one intend? Is this truly for my own misfortune, or might there be some other purpose behind his resolve? He stood watching.
(8) That hunter also, having arrived at that tree, spread out his net, scattered grains of grain, and remained hidden not far away. (9)
Then, Citragrīva, the king of pigeons, wandering through the sky with a retinue of a thousand pigeons, saw those grains of rice.
With his mind enticed by the prospect of food, he fell into the net along with his followers; they were all bound without exception by the snares of sinew.
Seeing this, the fowler was delighted at heart and, raising his club, ran toward them.
Citragrīva, seeing his own followers wandering here and there and being dragged toward the net by those with their variegated beaks and feet, said to them: "A great calamity has befallen us!
There is only one way out of this. All of you, becoming single-minded, must fly up into the air and go a very great distance; otherwise, it will be impossible to escape the net."
And so it was carried out by those who desired life: having taken up the net and left the path through the air at a distance of a single arrow-shot, they set forth into the sky.
The fowler, seeing the net being carried away by the birds and thinking, "This is unprecedented," ran with his face turned upward and concluded:
"These birds, acting in concert, are carrying off my net."
"But when they begin to quarrel, they will come under my control.
(2.186) Citragrīva, seeing him following so cruelly, began to move away quickly.
Laghupatanaka, too, abandoning all thought of food, followed the flock of pigeons out of curiosity, wondering: "What will this wicked soul do to the pigeons?"
(18) Citragrīva, having understood his intention, said to his companions: "This wicked hunter is pursuing us, following our tracks. Therefore, it is better for us to remain invisible.
[Flying far away,] let us go over the mountains, trees, and rugged terrain.
Then the birds vanished, taking water with them. When the hunter realized they had gone beyond the range of sight, he turned back in despair.
Citragrīva, seeing that they had turned back, said to them:
"O, that wicked hunter has indeed returned. Therefore, it is better for us also to turn back and go to Mahilārōpya.
There, in the north-eastern part, is my dear friend, a mouse named Hiraṇyaka."
"He dwells there.

Saying "So be it," they reached the vicinity of Hiraṇyaka's hole and gathered together.
Hiraṇyaka, too, though skilled in policy, lived there having made the hole have a hundred openings out of fear of misfortune; with a heart terrified by the swoop of birds, Hiraṇyaka remained hidden.
Citragrīva, having placed [himself] at the mouth of the burrow, said: "My good Hiranyaka, come this way.
Hearing that, Hiranyaka, remaining right inside the fortress of the burrow, asked: "Who are you?

Hearing this, his body bristling with joy and his heart filled with delight, Citragrīva came out in haste;

And because of which, by which, when, how, what,

"By this mind of yours, O Śākya, you shall even become the lord of the three worlds.

Having reflected thus, he descended from that tree, approached the entrance of the burrow, and called out to Hiraṇyaka by the name he had previously learned: "My good Hiraṇyaka, come here for a moment.

"Furthermore, if some misfortune should ever befall my fawn, you will find liberation from its side. Therefore, you ought to favor me with your friendship.

What is impossible cannot be done; what is possible can indeed be accomplished. A cart does not travel on water, nor is it moved by a boat on dry land. (12) Your virtues, even if unspoken, manifest themselves of their own accord.
"Even when being covered, the *mālatī* flower continues to emit its fragrance.

"Therefore, a fickle person undoubtedly ruins all undertakings. (14.
"Therefore, let us depart from this place of siege at the fortress.

Hiraṇyaka said: "O sir, how can I make friends with you, my enemy? And it is said:
One should not form an alliance with an enemy, even by means of a very firm treaty;
for water, however hot it may be, still extinguishes fire. (15)
The crow said: "O sir, I do not even have an audience with you; how then could there be enmity? Why then do you speak such an improper thing?
(Then, laughing) Hiraṇyaka replied: "Good sir, in this world there are two kinds of enmity observed in the treatises: innate and acquired. You are our innate enemy.
The crow said: "O sir, I wish to hear the definition of both types of enmity."

"Let that be told. He said: "O sir, that which arises from a cause is artificial (*kṛtrima*); it passes away through the application of appropriate means. Natural (*svābhāvika*) enmity, however, does not depart by any means whatsoever. Furthermore, that natural enmity is of two kinds:
enmity involving one party (*ekāṅga-vaira*) and enmity involving both parties (*ubhaya-vaira*). The crow asked: 'What is the distinction between those two?
He replied: 'That wherein they strike one another, devour one another, and [act] out of mutual injury—that is enmity involving both parties, such as that between lions and elephants.'"

When one who has already killed someone eats them, that person neither harms nor injures him, nor is he eaten; that is a one-sided enmity (*ekāṅgavaira*), occurring without cause, as in the case of horses and buffaloes, cats and mice, or snakes and mongooses.
Does the horse harm the buffalo, or the snake the mongoose, or the mouse the cat?

"What hope is there that this wicked man is a friend?

For the world is bound by the fear of loss of wealth. Whether it be a beloved one, or one cherished through many good deeds,

"The thought 'I have committed no offense' is not a cause for confidence;

(20.201) "Fluidity is the cause [of melting] for all metals; [instinct] is the cause for beasts and birds."

"Who else besides you, endowed with such qualities, could I have obtained? Thus, it would indeed be appropriate for me to enter into an agreement with you; otherwise, I shall destroy myself by fasting at your door."
I have been convinced by you; let it be as you desire.

Therefore, enough with such a means of sustaining life. (207)

"You shall go. He said: (76) "Not far from here, in the midst of a dense forest, there is a great lake. There dwells a dear friend of mine, a tortoise named Mantharaka, who has long been an old acquaintance. (77) He will nourish me with a variety of food, such as fish and other delicacies. Together with him, I shall spend my time happily and without anxiety.
(78) Having heard that, Hiraṇyaka said: "I too—" [208]
"Therefore, I shall come along with you; I too have grown weary of this world.
The crow asked, "What is the cause of your weariness?
Hiraṇyaka replied, "There is much to be said; having gone there, I will tell you everything."
At the very moment those words were spoken, the crow seized his friend with his beak and reached the vast lake.

Then, seeing the crow approaching from afar along with the mouse, Mantharaka—knowing the proper place and time—thought, "Who is this? and, fearing for himself, leapt from the sandbank and submerged in the water. Laghupatanaka, too, his heart agitated by the splash of the water, wondered, "What is this? He placed Hiraṇyaka back upon the sandbank and climbed a large tree, desiring to investigate further.

Standing there, he said: (84) "O Mantharaka, come! Come! I, your friend, the crow named Laghupatanaka, have arrived after a long time with great longing. Therefore, come and embrace me. (85) Having heard this and recognized him most clearly—with his body bristling with joy and his eyes overflowing with tears of bliss—Mantharaka quickly emerged from the water and embraced Laghupatanaka, who had climbed down from the tree, saying: "Forgive my offense that I did not recognize you. (86) Then, after he had joyfully offered hospitality to them both, he asked the crow: "Friend, where have you come from? How is it that you have come to this deserted forest having captured a mouse? [210] Kaś...?
"And this is the mouse.
The crow said: "This is the mouse named Hiraṇyaka;
even one who possessed a thousand tongues could not fully describe the extent of the virtues of this long-lived one."
"Affections last until the end of life, yet anger is momentary; even great-souled beings do not fail to practice selfless renunciation.

Having thus related the liberation of Citragrīva exactly as it occurred, as well as his own meeting with him, Mantharaka—astonished by hearing the greatness of Hiraṇyaka’s virtues—questioned Hiraṇyaka.
"By what kind of world-weariness, or by what cause of humiliation, have you resolved upon the abandonment of your own country, friends, kinsmen, and wife? (90)

Vayasa said: "I too asked him that very same question at first; however, he replied that there was much to be told and that he would explain it once he had gone there himself. He did not inform me either. Therefore, my dear Hiraṇyaka, let it now be told—how both of us may bring about the end of our mutual enmity. Then Hiraṇyaka related:
"In the southern country, there is a city named Mahilāropya. Not far from it is a monastery for wandering mendicants."

There lived a wandering mendicant named Cūḍakarṇa. At the time for alms, he would fill his begging bowl with various kinds of food from that city—specifically, savory and delicate preparations containing pieces of sugar-cane, molasses, and pomegranate—and having returned to his dwelling, he would sustain himself according to the rules. Then, setting aside the remainder of the food in his bowl and storing it well concealed, he would hang that bowl on a peg [213] for the sake of his attendant who would come at dawn, and go to sleep during the night.
(93) And I, leaping up, ate that food every day, and I lived there with my retinue upon it.

(94) Even though it was thus carefully guarded by me while I was eating it, that wandering mendicant became despondent; out of fear of me, he moved it from place to higher place. Nevertheless, I reached it without any effort at all and ate it.
(95) Now, as time was thus passing, once upon a time a wandering mendicant named Bṛhatsphig arrived as a guest of his dear friend.
(96) Cūḍakarṇa, having performed for him the hospitable rites beginning with a welcome, [observed that he had completed the period of his prescribed vows].
(97) Then, at night, he questioned Bṛhatsphija, who was seated on his bed: "Ever since you were separated from me, through which other lands or ascetic groves have you wandered?"

(98) He said: "Then once, having performed my ablutions at Puṣkara, the most excellent of great tīrthas, on the occasion of Mahākārttika, I was separated from you due to the crowd of a vast multitude of people. Thereafter, wandering along the Ganges in both favorable and unfavorable directions through Gaṅgādvāra, Prayāga, Vārāṇasī, and other places—in short, I beheld the entire circle of the earth as far as the ocean.
(99) And while I was there, Cūḍakarṇa, in order to frighten me, repeatedly struck and sounded his alms-bowl with a worn-out bamboo stick."
When an obstacle arose while he was speaking, Bṛhatsphiga became angry and said:
"I am telling you this out of respect for you; why are you so disrespectful (as if arrogant), indifferent to my story, and preoccupied with something else?"

Cūḍakarṇa (abashed) said: "My good man, you should not be angry; I am not disenchanted with the world. However, look: this mouse is my constant tormentor. Even though I hold my alms-bowl in a place of safety, it leaps up and climbs onto it, and eats whatever remains of the alms-food still there. I am unable to ward it off;
therefore, to frighten the mouse, I strike this worn-out bowl against it again and again. There is no other reason."
He said: "Is this a single mouse here, or are there other mice as well?
He replied: "What is the use of other mice? This one rogue alone constantly deceives me, like a wicked yogi.
Hearing this, the other said: "A mere mouse does not possess such power; there must be some underlying cause for this."
And it has been said:
"A mother would not, for no reason, barter sesame seeds for sesame seeds that have already had their husks removed; in this matter, there must be a purpose served by those very husked seeds. (27)
Cūḍākarṇa said: "And how was that? He replied:
"Once, during the approaching rainy season, I requested a certain Brahmin for lodging in a particular town (for the purpose of taking up residence), and I stayed in his house.
Then, on another day—"
Having woken at dawn, I listened attentively to the conversation between a Brahmin and his wife as they spoke from behind a lattice.
There, the Brahmin said:
"O Brahminī, tomorrow will be a festival day; on that occasion, you must provide a meal for Brahmins according to your means."

He said with words of many harsh syllables: "How do you have the power to feed brahmins, being so utterly destitute? Having been addressed thus, he remained silent like one cast into a well. After a long time, he spoke again: "Brahmin woman," she said, "how was that? He replied:
"In a certain district there was a hunter who lived by meat. Once, having risen at dawn with his bow strung, he set out into the forest to hunt deer."
Having quickly killed a deer and taken its meat, he was returning when [116] he saw a buffalo—a beast of great affection for its calf—with its horns uprooted and its body smeared with clumps of mud.

[117] Seeing it, impelled by an auspicious omen, fear came upon him; turning back and his movement obstructed by the buffalo, he threw the deer-meat, which had been rolled into a ball, onto the ground.
[118] Drawing his bow, he discharged at him an arrow smeared with poison; having pierced the joint of his neck, it emerged from the opposite side.

[119] Even the boar, though stunned by the blow, exerted its utmost speed and struck him in the vicinity of the refuse heap in such a way that he fell lifeless upon the ground, his body split in three.
(Then, having killed the hunter, the boar also passed away due to the pain of the arrow-wound.

(120) Immediately thereafter, a jackal named Dīrgharāva, whose belly was emaciated by hunger, while wandering in search of food, arrived at that place and saw the deer, the hunter, and the boar [all dead].
(121) Seeing them, he was delighted and thought: "Ah! Fate is favorable to me; thus, this unexpected meal has presented itself."
(122) Therefore, I consume it in such a way that my sustenance lasts for many days.
For food and drink do not arise even once a hundred times for embodied beings;
having obtained abundant food and drink, one should employ it gradually. 29.
"In that case, I shall first eat this sinew-noose attached to the tip of the bow [used by] the hunters of deer and boars through their deceitful trickery.
Having said this, he [climbed] upon the bow—
Having placed the tethering-rope in his mouth, he began to chew it;
and when the tethering-rope was severed by the bow, [the rope struck] his palate—
"In that country, he was torn apart and met his death.
(126) Therefore I say: "One must always make an accumulation.
(127) Having heard this, the Brahmin woman said: "If that is so, then I have a small amount of sesame and a small amount of rice."

(128) "Therefore, rising at dawn, go to the forest to fetch firewood, *kuśa* grass, and other necessities; I too, along with this disciple Kāmandakī, shall prepare the sacrificial oblation for the three Brahmins.
(129) Then, at daybreak, she had those sesame seeds plucked out and entrusted them to Kāmandakī [with the words], "Protect them," as they stood in the heat of the sun.

"Father. (130) In the meantime, because she was preoccupied with household chores and thus inattentive, those sesame seeds were approached and eaten by a dog and scattered. (131) Seeing that, she said: "Kāmandaki, you have not been careful; an obstacle has arisen for the Brahmins' satiation. (132) Nevertheless, go; having exchanged these [already-plucked] sesame seeds for black sesame seeds, return quickly;
(I shall prepare a dish of black sesame porridge alone)."

And so, when it had been carried out, I arrived at that very house for alms; at that same house, Kāmandakī had also entered for the purpose of selling sesame seeds and said, "Let these sesame seeds be taken. While the transaction was being concluded, the householder arrived. He asked, "How are the sesame seeds being exchanged?"
She said to him: "I have obtained sesame seeds at a good price—both white and black.
Then he (laughing) said: "There must be a reason for this.
Therefore I say: "The mother Śāṇḍilī did not do so without cause."
Having spoken thus, the wandering mendicant said: "Cūḍākarṇa, even in this case, there must be some reason why the mouse, whose power remains unimpeded, is eating the alms-food."
(136) "Is there some kind of spade?
He replied, "Certainly there is; this Suhastikā is made of all the elements of the world.
(137) And having tied his girdle near it, with his lips bitten together, he asked: "Which way is his path of movement?"
When he had spoken thus, he began to dig my hole with that spade.
And I, having heard their private conversation right from the start, cast aside my necklace and remained there, overcome with curiosity.
(139) But when he began to search for the fortress, I realized: "This wicked soul has discovered the entrance to the middle cavity.
(140) I, too, had obtained gold previously deposited by a certain virtuous person; because of that wealth, I considered myself to be powerful.

(141) That wicked man also, having discovered it by following the tracks, seized the wealth and returned to his dwelling. He said to Cūḍākarṇa: "O Brahmin, here is that gold of his; by the power of [his] heart, he can leap even to a place that is impossible [to reach]. Then, having divided [the wealth] into equal halves, they remained living happily.

(142) And having fallen into despondency over this, I thought: "Perhaps, while I am staying here, they might light a lamp and, having found me without a doubt, kill me. Therefore, I established another secure location from that place.

(143) Furthermore, other followers of mine came and said to me: "O noble Hiraṇyaka, we who dwell in your vicinity are extremely tormented by hunger; we do not have even a morsel of food. Even though the day has ended, nothing has been obtained by us. Therefore, you ought to satisfy us even now. (144) Having said, "So be it," I went with them to their dwelling.
(145) Then, upon hearing the words "our own possession," Cūḍakarṇa also began once more to strike the alms-bowl with his worn-out bamboo staff.
(146) He was addressed by him: "Why even now, while that outcaste remains, do you keep shaking the staff? Enough!"
Then he said: "Good sir, this mouse, my enemy, keeps coming back again and again.
Thereupon, the guest laughed and said: "Friend, do not fear; with his wealth has gone his spirit for leaping about.
For such is the condition of all living beings."
Then, having heard that, overcome with anger, I leaped up specifically toward my alms-bowl; but before reaching the ground, I fell down.
Seeing me, that enemy of mine laughed and said to Cūḍākarṇa: "Friend, look, look at this marvel! For it is said:
'Everyone becomes powerful through wealth, and through wealth one becomes wise. Behold this wicked mouse, who has returned to the common state of his own kind. (30)
"Therefore, O friend, you may go without fear.
That which was the cause of his power to fly has now come into the hands of both of us.

I reflected within my mind: "He speaks the truth; for today, being devoid of my own power and lacking the impulse of courage, I do not have the strength to even raise my arm, let alone the power to fly even a finger's breadth upward."

And I hear the conversation of the wandering mendicants among themselves: "Come, let us go; this man is not even capable of filling his own belly, much less those of others. So what is the use of serving him?"

Then, having reflected thus, I went to my own dwelling. At the time of dawn, all [my followers] went into the presence of my rivals, saying, "He is a pauper. Not even one of those attendants who had behaved in such a manner came into my presence. And I saw them: upon seeing me face to face, those very same attendants of mine were playing with my rivals, shouting "kila-kila" and clapping their hands together. And I thought: "So it is! [232]
He who has wealth has friends; he who has wealth has kinsmen;
he who has wealth is a man in this world; and he who has wealth is a wise man.
For indeed, for a man of little intelligence who is deprived of wealth—
All activities are cut short, like small streams in the summer heat;
friends, sons, wives, and even brothers abandon one who is destitute of wealth.
They indeed return once more to that which possesses meaning;
for in this world, wealth is the kinsman of a man.
The house of one without a son is empty, and the heart of one who has no true friend is empty.

For the fool, all directions are empty; for the poor man, everything is empty. 34. [233] Those very same senses are unimpaired, that very same name remains, and that very same intelligence exists with unimpeded speech.
That very same person, deprived of the warmth of wealth,
becomes someone else in an instant— this is truly extraordinary.
One may dwell for a long time where one's pride is honored, but one should never take refuge with one whose pride has been shattered.
One should avoid even a celestial chariot together with the gods if it is devoid of honor.
(36) Better than birth as a beggar is birth as a tree that is humpbacked, scarred by axes, its bark stripped away by wild animals, and standing in barren soil. (37)

Hoarseness in the throat, perspiration on the face, pallor, and trembling—these very signs belong to one who is dying, yet they also belong to one who begs. They are the abode of misfortune, the thief of the intellect, and the locus of false conceptualization. 38.
Begging is a synonym for death, an abode of wretchedness, a supreme repository of fear, embodied insignificance, and the very refuge of calamities; it robs the spirited of their luster.
Indeed, for the high-minded, I see no state more wretched than begging, even compared to hell.
Moreover:
"One who lacks wealth falls into shame; one overcome by shame is deprived of his splendor."
One devoid of splendor is overcome; from being overcome, he falls into despondency;
being despondent, he comes to grief; with a grieving mind, his intellect perishes;
and being bereft of intellect, he goes to destruction—alas, such is the state of death, the abode of all calamities.
Better to place both hands in the mouth of a serpent filled with rage,
or better to drink poison and fall asleep in the abode of Death.
It is better that my body be cast from the slope of this best of mountains and shatter into a hundred pieces,
than that my soul be gratified by wealth obtained from base people. It is better that the fire be satiated with my life-breaths while I am destitute of riches.
A person who has strayed from right conduct is wretched when he begs.
Now, this being the case, by what other means could life be sustained?
Could it be by theft? Even that is more painful than [the former], because it involves taking the sweat of others. For this reason:
It is better to remain silent than to speak a falsehood;
it is better for men to be impotent than to approach another's wife;
it is better to give up one's life than to take delight in the words of the malicious.
Better is the eating of alms than the pleasure of tasting the wealth of others. (43) Now, what is the point of sustaining myself on the food of another? Alas! That too is a second door to death.
For one who is sick, a long-time traveler, an eater of others' food, and a sleeper in another's dwelling, that which is life is death, and that which is death is his rest.

"In every way, I shall make that very wealth my own. For I have seen that those two evil-minded men disregarded the deposit out of greed for the money. I shall take that wealth to my own fortress, so that by the power of that wealth, my sovereignty may once again be as it was before. Having thus resolved, he went there at night; while the other was under the influence of sleep, Maya crept close and bored a hole into the chest. Just as he had finished making the opening, the ascetic woke up.
Then, I was struck on the head with a worn-out wooden club by him.
(161) By some stroke of remaining life-force, I emerged [from the trap] and entered my burrow; I did not die.

(162) After a long time, having recovered my wits and regained my strength, I approached the presence of the Lord of Serpents, whereupon that merciless man struck me on the head with a staff in such a way that even today, for those who have fallen asleep, there is such a trembling at the mere thought of it.
And behold this wound upon my head, inflicted at that very moment.
And it is well said:

"Having encountered a calamity difficult to overcome, which brings the danger of the destruction of all one's life, one whose fear is imminent does not perceive his own misfortune and longs for his life."

But having emerged from that, for the sake of wealth, he enters yet another calamity; for life, wealth, means of accomplishment, and thoughts are all mutually dependent stakes. Knowledge is the eye, but not sight; good character is noble birth, but not birth in a noble family; contentment is prosperity, and wisdom is the desisting from what ought not to be done. 46.
All prosperity belongs to him whose mind is content;
for one whose feet are covered by sandals, is not the entire earth as if covered with leather? (47) The happiness of those whose minds are peaceful and who are satiated by the nectar of contentment—

Whence could that [happiness] come for those greedy for wealth who run hither and thither? (48) A hundred yojanas is not far for one being carried along; but for one content with grass, there is no regard even for wealth already in hand. (49)
Therefore, in every respect, discernment (*pariccheda*) alone is superior regarding an object that cannot be accomplished. And it has been said:
"What is dharma? Compassion for living beings. What is happiness in this world for a creature? Freedom from disease. What is affection? True existence. What is wisdom? Discernment. (50)

(Thus. Having reflected thus, I went to a deserted forest and saw Citragrīva bound with a rope; and having liberated him—(through the arising of our merit)—I was favored by this Laghupatanaka out of his devotion to friendship.
Just then, this (Laghupatanaka) approached me.
"I have come here for the purpose of seeing you. Thus, I have arrived in your presence along with him. This is the cause of my despondency. Moreover:
With deer whose essence is passion, the three worlds—including gods, asuras, and humans—take their meal here until midday. (51)
Even after conquering the entire earth or falling into a degraded state, if one desires to enjoy life at the proper time, even a grain of rice can be obtained.
For its sake, what wise person indeed would perform a contemptible deed?
"His continuity of misfortune, persisting day and night, is failing.
53.[241] Having heard this, Mantharaka comforted him: "My good friend, you should not despair because I have abandoned my own country; for you are wise—why are you bewildered? Moreover:
even after studying the scriptures, people remain fools."
But the man who acts is the wise one;
for does medicine, merely by its name, make a sick person healthy when it has not been prepared? 54. [242]

For one who lacks resolve does not achieve even the slightest merit through the practice of knowledge; indeed, can a lamp, though held in the hand of a blind man, bring back an object that has already vanished? (55) Men beg by giving, but they are surely slain by killing.
And having been cast down, they perish when human fortune turns away.
Nor should it be thought that those who have fallen from their position no longer shine—just as teeth, hair, nails, and men [may appear so after being removed]. 56.
Knowing this, however, a wise person should not abandon his own country.

For what place is considered a foreign land to a courageous and high-minded man, and what is his own domain? Whatever region he takes refuge in, that very place he makes resplendent with his great prowess.
When a lion enters the forest with his weapons of teeth, claws, and jaws, it is there that he quenches his own thirst with the blood of slain lordly elephants.
Therefore, my good sir, you must always be intent upon exertion; for wealth and enjoyments belong to those who are industrious—where else would they go? Moreover:

Like a frog to a water-hole, like a bird to a full lake, helpers, wealth, and success come to one who exerts effort of their own accord. (59) Fortune herself desires to dwell with one who is endowed with energy, who is not dilatory, who knows the proper method of action, who is unattached to vices, who is brave, grateful, and firm in friendship. (60) But Fortune does not wish to clothe herself in one who lacks resolve, who is lazy, who relies on fate, and who is devoid of courage—just as a young woman does not wish to embrace an old husband. (61)

"In this world, even a man of poor intellect is renowned for his prowess; yet one who possesses sound judgment is not honored by a king, even if he is as capable as Bṛhaspati, provided he lacks vigor in action. (62) Although you are devoid of wealth, you are endowed with wisdom, energy, and power, and are thus unlike ordinary men. How so? For a steadfast man, even without riches, attains positions that are elevated by great respect."
Even when surrounded by riches, the miser falls into a state of humiliation;
for a dog does not attain the lion-like splendor that arises from its own nature and is vast due to the acquisition of a multitude of qualities, even if it wears a necklace of artificial gold. 63.
He who is a mass of valor, courage, and fortitude endowed with the power of enthusiasm,
perceives the ocean as no larger than a cow’s footprint and the king of mountains as always resembling the peak of an anthill.
Fortune herself approaches that man who is not of feeble spirit.

(64) Neither is Mount Meru with its exceedingly high peaks, nor the netherworld Rasātala which is not too deep, nor the great ocean which has no further shore, unattainable for those whose resolve is firm. (65)
"What is this pride of yours regarding prosperity? Why do you fall into despondency when it has passed away?
Like balls struck by the hand, the rises and falls of human beings are like the bubbles on water—youth and wealth are entirely unstable. For:"
Shadows vanish like the affection of the wicked; new crops, women, youth, and wealth are enjoyable for only a brief moment.
Therefore, my good friend Hiranyaka, knowing this, even though your wealth has been taken away—
One should not give way to distress. And it has been said:
"That which is not to be will not be; that which is to be cannot be otherwise. Why is this antidote, which destroys the poison of anxiety, not drunk? 68.
(173) Therefore, abandon entirely this agitation caused by worrying about your livelihood; remain at ease.
He who has made the swans white, the parrots green, and the peacocks variegated—he shall provide for your livelihood. 69.
One who has met with misfortune should not grieve over it,
nor should one indulge in joy upon obtaining happiness; for this is simply the ripening of past karma that has been produced.
That [result], whether auspicious or inauspicious, inevitably comes to pass for human beings.
Therefore, with clear minds, one should daily perform even a small amount of dharma consisting of vows, observances, and fasting. 70. [246]

Death constantly strikes at the vital breaths of living beings, despite even the greatest effort being made; there is no other treasure equal to generosity. 71. There is no other treasure equal to generosity.
What happiness is there equal to contentment? Where is there an ornament equal to virtuous conduct?
There is no gain on earth equal to health. 72.
(174) What more need be said? This is your own home; therefore, with a tranquil and undisturbed mind, you should cultivate affection here together with me, just as before.

Time is indeed certain. (175) Having heard that [principle], which follows the meaning of many treatises and was spoken by Mantharaka, Laghupatanaka’s face blossomed with joy, and he attained great satisfaction: "O noble Mantharaka, you are endowed with qualities worthy of being sought as a refuge; for by your very act of assisting Hiraṇyaka, supreme contentment has been produced in my mind. What wonder is there in this? And it is said: Only they drink the essence of happiness; only they are truly living beings; only they are virtuous men."

Those who rejoice together with their friends—rejoicing with those who rejoice, dear ones with those who are dear—even though they possess power, they are indeed destitute. 73. For even those who have sovereignty are truly poor.

Those whose souls were carried away by greed have rendered their efforts fruitless and their lives devoid of essence, for they did not offer Fortune— adorned with the voluntary embrace of their friends— as a gift. 74.

The virtuous alone are always the means for the virtuous to cross over calamities; just as only elephants are capable of bearing the burden of other elephants mired in the mud. (75) You must always protect those of noble character, even at the risk of your own life.

For those of great fortune, the sole fruit of obtaining a body is indeed the favoring of others. (76) He alone among men on earth is praiseworthy, he alone has entered into the vow of the virtuous, from whom neither suppliants nor those seeking refuge depart with their hopes shattered or turned away in disappointment. (77)
Now, while they were thus conversing, a deer named Citrāṅga—terrified by a hunter and afflicted by thirst—arrived at that vast lake.
Seeing him approaching, their hearts trembling with fear, they began to flee.
As he rushed forward, desiring water, and was about to enter, there arose the sound of the clashing waters.
Pān—(179) Mantharaka has quickly submerged himself in the water from the sandbank.
(180) Hiraṇyaka, too, with an agitated mind, has entered a hollow in a tree. (181) Laghupatanaka, desiring to know what this was, has flown up and climbed a large tree.
(182) Citrāṅga, too, remained right near the bank out of fear for himself.

(183) Then Laghupatanaka, having flown up into the sky and surveyed the circle of the earth for a distance of one *yojana*, perched again upon the tree and said to Mantharaka: "Come, come! You have nothing to fear from anywhere. I have seen that there is only a grass-eating deer at the lake."
"I have come here seeking water.
Hearing this, all three of them gathered there as well.
Then he said to that deer: "Good sir, drink the water to your heart's content."
"Your purpose having been accomplished, you ought to come here.

Taking those words to heart, Citrāṅga reflected: "I have not even the slightest fear from these; why? For the tortoise has power only as long as he remains in the water, while the mouse and the crow feed only upon dead creatures and small vermin. Thinking, "Therefore, I shall follow them," he joined their company.
After Manthara had addressed him with a welcome and other hospitable greetings, he said to Citrāṅga, "Is it well with you? He replied, "How have you come to this dense forest?
Citrāṅga said, "I am weary of this life of pleasure;
being pursued here and there by hunters, I have come here out of fear."
"Therefore, I desire to establish friendship with you.
Mantharaka replied: "Good sir, do not fear; this house is yours. Dwell here as long as you wish, free from all obstacles.
Then, having taken their meals according to their own desires, they all gathered together constantly in the vast shade of the trees, [engaged in] the exposition of many treatises.
For those whose minds were intent on one another, time passed in mutual affection.
Then, once upon a time, Citraṅga did not arrive at the appointed hour.
Not seeing him, their minds became agitated by ill-omened signs that had arisen at that moment; suspecting some misfortune for him, they could find no composure.
Then Mantharaka said to Laghupatanaka: "Since you are endowed with the power for this task, you are well-acquainted with it; therefore, leap up and find out where Citrāṅgada is.
Having heard that, Laghupatanaka flew up, went not very far, and saw Citrāṅgada at a water-entry point, bound by a strong leather noose suspended from a stake.
Approaching him, he said with dejection: "My good friend, how have you fallen into this calamity?

Citrāṅga replied: "My good friend, this is no time for reproach; my death has already come upon me. Therefore, do not delay. For you are endowed with strength, whereas you are unskilled in the art of cutting snares.
So go quickly and bring Hiraṇyaka. He too—
"Capable of cutting the noose without effort.
Laghupātanaka went to Mantharaka and Hiraṇyaka, informed them of the nature of Citrāṅga’s capture,
and very quickly Hiraṇyaka arrived.
Seeing Citrāṅga in that state, Hiraṇyaka, overcome with distress, said to him: "Friend, you possess the eye of wisdom; how did you fall into this calamity?
He replied: "Friend, what is the use of asking this? Fate is indeed powerful."
And it has been said:
