"He who, without understanding the true nature of a matter, falls under the sway of anger, shall soon fall away from his friend, just as the Brahmin did from the mongoose. (1)
The princes asked, "And how was that? Viṣṇuśarman replied:
"In the land of Gauḍa there lived a certain Brāhmaṇa of noble lineage named Devaśarman. His wife was a Brāhmaṇa woman named Yajñadattā."

(Sometimes, by the power of former merit,) she became pregnant. Seeing this, Devaśarman attained great satisfaction and thought to himself: "A great blessing has come upon me for the sake of obtaining offspring. He then said to the Brahmin woman: "O blessed lady, you have achieved your purpose."

“You shall give birth to a son, and I, having many desires, shall perform for him the purificatory rites such as the *garbhādhāna*, the *jātakarman*, and the naming ceremony; he shall be the bearer of my lineage.

(8) Thus addressed, the Brāhmaṇī replied: “Who knows whether it will be a boy or not? It is not proper to speak thus regarding what is unseen. One should not form desires at the very outset. And it has been said:
‘The man who wishes to engage in thought concerning the future...’”
He lies on the ground white as Somaśarman’s father. He asked: "What is that story? She said: "There was a certain son of a Brahmin who was proficient in the sciences."
He had a regular meal at the house of a certain merchant.

Whenever he did not eat there, he would receive a small measure of groats (*saktusetikā*). Taking these home, he would pour them into a jar and set it aside. In this way, after a long time, the jar became completely full of groats.
Once, while that jar was placed on a wall-peg, the Brahmin, having gone to bed and awakened from his daytime sleep, found himself lying beneath it and thought to himself:
"Grain is very expensive, let alone cooked food or flour.
However, I have flour worth about twenty rūpakas.
By selling it, I will obtain ten goats for two rūpakas each."
They will give birth after six months, and their offspring likewise [will be born in six months].
After five years, they will become numerous, numbering four hundred.
And it is heard in the world that for four goats, one cow is obtained—[a young cow, with a living calf, yielding much milk, and endowed with all excellent qualities].
"With those very goats, I shall exchange for a hundred cows.
And when they have given birth, some of them will become oxen; by means of them, having practiced agriculture, I shall produce much grain."
From its sale, there will be abundant gold;
I shall construct a beautiful house made of bricks and enclosed by a wall.
Seeing that great fortune of mine—abounding in male and female slaves and complete with all household utensils—some most worthy Brahmin will surely give me a beautiful daughter.
And in that [time], by the increase of our merit, I shall give birth to a long-lived, healthy son who will uphold the lineage.
Having performed for him the birth-rites and other ceremonies according to the rules, I shall give him the name Somaśarman.
And when the boy has grown up, the Brahmin woman, foremost in household duties, [will attend to] the arrival of the cows...
If at that time the boy does not protect [her] properly due to negligence,
then I, my heart overcome by affection for my son, will strike that brahmin woman with a raised club.

Thus, while remaining in meditative absorption, he whirled a club and struck that jar, by which it was shattered into a hundred pieces and cast down with its contents spilled; then that brahmin, his body greyed by flour and dust, imagining himself to have risen from a dream-like state, was overcome with extreme embarrassment and public laughter.
Therefore I say: "One should not worry about what has not yet come; when the task is seen [to be accomplished]... (402)
Action proceeds; there is no painting without a wall. And when the time for birth was fulfilled, the Brahmin woman gave birth to a boy endowed with auspicious marks.

(29) Now, when ten days had passed since the birth, the Brāhmaṇī, having entrusted the infant—who had already been performed with the birth rites—to his father for protection, went to a nearby river for the purpose of purifying herself after cleansing her soiled garments. (30) The Brāhmaṇa, too, out of poverty and a sense of shared hardship, remained there alone and protected the boy. (31) Then, a maidservant of the queen was sent from the royal palace to summon the Brāhmaṇa on account of some business concerning the king’s family. (32) Being called, that Brāhmaṇa, tormented by his innate poverty, thought to himself: (33) "If I do not go quickly now—" [403]
Someone else takes the alms-offering; there is no protector for the boy.

"What shall I do? (34). While things were thus situated, that brahmin departed, leaving behind the mongoose—who was like a son to her in the house of the domestic fire-altar (*agṛihotra-śaraṇa*)—and who had been raised on grains of rice and other such food. (35). Before long, the mongoose saw a black cobra emerging from a hole in the ground and approaching the vicinity of the boy. (36). Upon seeing it—with eyes bloodshot with rage, its face, teeth, and tail quivering violently—it sprang up suddenly and pounced upon it, tearing it into pieces. (37). With its mouth and feet smeared with blood, it saw the brahmin approaching and felt exceedingly gratified in its mind. [404]
He went outside to report this. (38) Then that Brahmin, who had acted without due consideration, saw him with his face smeared with blood by those mongooses and thought:
"How is it that my little son has been devoured by this one? and [struck] him with a staff.

He struck him. (39) Having killed him, immediately thereafter, when that brahmin had entered his house, he saw his son sleeping there with all his limbs intact, and the black snake nearby, cut into pieces. [405]
"Alas! I am ruined, I of dull intellect; what an unworthy deed have I committed! he said, beating his own heart.
Then the Brahmin woman arrived and, seeing the weeping Brahmin, observed the dead mongoose and the snake cut into a hundred pieces, and said to him: "What is this, Brahmin? How did this happen?
Thereupon, the Brahmin related the entire account. Seeing this, the Brahmin woman fell into great despair and said to the Brahmin:
"A man should not act upon what is poorly seen, poorly understood, poorly heard, or poorly examined, just as was done by the barber. He said, "What is this story? She replied:

Once upon a time, in a certain city, there was a merchant’s son whose wealth and lineage had perished and who was overwhelmed by poverty. From his childhood, he had been raised in the house of a disciple by an elderly nurse with whom he lived; thus, he was brought up by that aged female servant. At the very onset of the first watch of the night, he sighed deeply and thought: "Alas! How long will this poverty endure? Having reflected thus, he went to sleep.
And at the end of the night, he saw a dream. Having approached, he was awakened by three monks and addressed thus:
"Good sir, at the time of dawn we shall come to you in this very form.
For this reason: there are three treasures deposited by your ancestors."
"Struck by you with a club, we shall become dirhams.
You must not show compassion in this matter.

Reflecting on that dream even as he was waking at the time of dawn, he said to his nurse: "Today, mother, you must be constantly diligent; the household chores such as sweeping with cow dung must be performed, and food must be given to three Brahmins according to your means."
"I too shall bring the barber.
When this had been carried out, the barber arrived for the purpose of shaving his beard and clipping his nails.
Once the work on the beard was finished, he [the king] observed his own feet through a stratagem.
Then the merchant’s son, seeing that mendicant, carried out exactly as he had been instructed. And those riches were successfully acquired.
As that flood of wealth was being brought in, the caravan leader’s son gave three hundred dīnāras to Divākīrṇa for his gratification and for the sake of maintaining secrecy.

The barber also, seeing them, went to his own home out of a false attachment [to his wealth] and thought: "I too shall kill three mendicants with a club and turn them into a triple-treasure. Then, taking up a club, he remained there in ambush. Immediately thereafter, by the power of karma, three monks arrived for alms.
"Then, having been struck with a club by the barber, he was killed; yet the treasure was not found.
Immediately thereafter, the barber was dragged away by the king’s men, taken away, and impaled upon a stake.
Therefore I say: 'That which is poorly seen and poorly understood...'"
Thus ends the fifth chapter, titled "Acting Without Due Examination."
